expected_edges.rationale: A cross-file call through an explicit import. The extractor must bind it to the project node rather than leaving it external, and must attribute it to the calling method rather than the module.
The faithful import record. Python import targets stay external because the specifier is what was imported; the corresponding call is what resolves to a project node.
A module defining its own function. The most basic structural claim the graph makes; if this is missing, nothing downstream can resolve.
A configuration file defining a key node. Required so a configuration read has something to bind to.
The one key the loader actually reads, bound from a string literal subscript. This is the relation with the highest over-binding risk, which is why its forbidden counterpart is the sibling key.
A documentation reference that names a symbol unambiguously in backticks. Scored only at EXTRACTED confidence or better, so an ambiguous doc match cannot be credited as a correct binding.

AMBIGUOUS NAME. Two modules define `parse`; the import names one. The call must bind to the imported module's definition, so the extractor has to consult the import rather than match on the bare symbol name.

SCHEMA/CONFIG COLLISION. A second config file shares the key name `retry_budget_ms` with svc/config.json. This reader touches only its own file's `audit_sink`, so the binder must be scoped to the file the literal names.
The colliding key node itself must exist, or the collision control below has nothing to over-bind TO and would pass vacuously.

CONSTRUCTOR. `Session(token)` binds to the Session CLASS node. Its id is the bare file path because a file whose only top-level construct is one class does not get a separate module node -- the class takes the file's id (contrast svc/transports.py, which has two classes and keeps a module node). The binding is correct; the identity collapse is recorded as known gap `single_class_file_identity`.

TEST BOUNDARY. A test calling production code is a genuine edge and is recorded. The target is the Worker class node, whose id is the bare file path for the same single-class reason as svc/session.py.

SAME-NAME METHODS. Two classes define `send`; the receiver type is fixed by the constructor on the same expression, so the faithful edge names HttpTransport's method. The extractor currently resolves the receiver to the correct CLASS and stops there, which is recorded as known gap `method_level_receiver_attribution` -- the discrimination between the two classes is real, the member-level attribution is not yet.

forbidden_edges.rationale: A sibling method in the same class that calls nothing. An extractor that attributes calls to the enclosing class rather than the enclosing method would emit this, which is why it is the forbidden counterpart to the expected call.
A self-import. The module that DEFINES the symbol must never be recorded as importing it; this fires if import candidates are collected without checking the declaring file.
A cross-file definition. Fires if definition edges are keyed by symbol name rather than by declaring file, which would let two files claim each other's symbols.

The sibling configuration key the loader never reads. This is the sharpest control in the corpus: a binder that matches a configuration FILE and then attaches every key in it, rather than matching the specific literal used at the read site, emits exactly this edge.
A method the guide never mentions. Fires if a documentation reference binds to every symbol in a mentioned class rather than to the symbol actually named.
The AMBIGUOUS-NAME control. Fires if the extractor binds a call to every definition sharing the name instead of resolving through the import.

The seeded `cpu_count` control named in AC-2. `os.cpu_count()` is a stdlib call; the project happens to define a function with the same bare name. Binding by name alone wires an external API to unrelated project code, which is the single most misleading false edge this graph can produce.
The SAME-NAME METHOD control. Fires if a method call binds to every class declaring that method rather than to the receiver's own.

The SCHEMA/CONFIG COLLISION control. Two config files declare `retry_budget_ms`; this reader reads neither of them, and certainly not the other file's. Fires if configuration binding matches on key name across files.
The CONSTRUCTOR control. Fires if instantiation is treated as calling every method of the class rather than constructing it.

The SAME-NAME METHOD control restated at CLASS granularity, which is where the extractor actually binds. Without this the method-level control alone would pass vacuously, because no method-level edge is emitted for either class.

known_gaps.rationale: Isolated by controlled experiment: with `retry_budget_ms` present in BOTH svc/config.json and svc/audit-config.json the binding disappears; removing the duplicate key from audit-config.json restores it, with nothing else changed. The binder fails SAFE (it drops rather than mis-binding, so no false positive), but it loses an edge whose owning file the source literal names unambiguously via CONFIG_PATH. Recall loss, not a correctness violation.

The receiver resolves to the correct class -- the extractor emits `svc/dispatch.py::dispatch -> svc/transports.py::HttpTransport` at RECEIVER_RESOLVED confidence, and never touches QueueTransport -- but the edge is not attributed to the specific member invoked. Impact analysis therefore reaches the class, not the method.
